```{r}
#| label: functions

# marginaleffects::avg_slopes() with common arguments
.avg_slopes <- function(model) {
  avg_slopes(
    model,
    variables = "crit_sick",
    by = "gender",
    # Need to specify df to get a t-test rather than a z test
    df = model$df.residual,
    # For one-sided p.value
    equivalence = c(-Inf, 0)
  )
}

# Common style for tables
.tt <- function(data, ...) {
  data |>
    tt(...) |>
    style_tt(
      align = "l",
      fontsize = 0.8
    ) |>
    style_tt(
      i = "notes",
      align = "l",
      fontsize = 0.8
    ) |>
    style_tt(
      i = 0,
      align = "c",
      fontsize = 0.8
    ) |>
    format_tt(replace = "") |>
    theme_tt(theme = "spacing", rowsep = 0)
}

# Table of coefficients from test [t1, t2, t3, t4]
tbl_coef <- function(
  data = dat_fit,
  test = NULL,
  cols = gender, # gender [t1-3] | hypothesis [t4]
  p = p.value.nonsup # one-sided or p.value for t4
) {
  data |>
    select(group, {{ test }}) |>
    unnest({{ test }}) |>
    mutate(
      p = {{ p }},
      across(
        c(where(is.numeric), -p),
        ~ number(.x, .01)
      ),
      Estimate = str_glue(
        "{estimate} ({std.error}) [{conf.low}, {conf.high}], ",
        "{pvalue(p, add_p = TRUE)}"
      ),
    ) |>
    select(Target = group, {{ cols }}, Estimate) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = {{ cols }}, values_from = Estimate) |>
    .tt(
      notes = list(
        "Numbers indicate point estimate (SE) [95% CI]"
      )
    ) |>
    group_tt(
      i = paste("Hypothesis", c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4))
    ) |>
    style_tt(
      i = c(1, 6, 9, 15),
      bold = TRUE,
      align = "c"
    )
}
```


# Results

```{r}
#| label: data-qualtrics-wrangle
#| output: false

# Load data with good names
# Hack to skip second row but include names
dat <- read_excel(
  Sys.getenv("PATH_DATA_RAW"),
  skip = 2,
  col_names = names(read_excel(Sys.getenv("PATH_DATA_RAW")))
) |>
  clean_names() |>
  rename(pid = response_id) |>
  filter(consent == 1, age >= 18) |>
  select(
    -c(
      start_date:recorded_date,
      distribution_channel, user_language,
      consent, q50, comments
    )
  )

# Write reduced data for sharing
dir.create("data", FALSE)
write_csv(dat, "data/data-raw.csv")
codebook <- read_excel("data/codebook.xlsx") |>
  clean_names()

# Count exclusions
# "We will exclude from the analysis participants who
# (1) fail the attention check,
# (2) are not native speakers of English,
# (3) do not live in the US, and
# (4) have missing responses on 5 or more trials on the detection task for contagious disease (i.e., to be included a participant must have responded to at least 10 of the 14 trials)."
s <- list()
s$total_before_exclusions <- nrow(dat)
s$not_attention <- nrow(dat[dat$attention_check != 4, ])
s$not_english <- nrow(dat[dat$language != 1, ])
s$not_us <- nrow(dat[dat$residence != 1, ])
# Participants responded to one of two sets, so always have 14 missings
dat <- dat |>
  mutate(
    missing = apply(
      across(x1_sick_v1:x14_sick_v2),
      1,
      \(x) sum(is.na(x)) - 14
    )
  )
s$missing <- nrow(dat[dat$missing > 0, ])

# Apply exclusion criteria
# todo: Enable for real data
dat <- dat |>
  filter(
    attention_check == 4,
    language == 1,
    residence == 1,
    missing < 5
  )
s$total_after_exclusions <- nrow(dat)

# Remove unnecessary variables
dat <- dat |>
  select(
    -c(language, residence, attention_check),
    pid
  )

# Create SDT metrics

## Correct responses
sdt_code <- codebook |>
  filter(str_detect(variable_name, "sick|criminal")) |>
  select(name = variable_name, correct_response) |>
  mutate(name = str_c("x", name))

## Separate table for SDT tasks
sdt <- dat |>
  select(pid, contains("_sick_"), contains("criminal"))

## (Critical: see codebook, 1=Yes, 2=No)
## Join SDT responses with correct response info
## And recode values
sdt <- sdt |>
  pivot_longer(-pid, values_to = "response") |>
  # Drop rows with missing response
  drop_na(response) |>
  left_join(sdt_code, by = "name") |>
  mutate(
    response = factor(
      response,
      levels = c(2, 1),
      labels = c("No", "Yes")
    ),
    truth = if_else(
      correct_response %in% c("sick", "criminal"),
      "Yes",
      "No"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    accuracy = as.integer(response == truth),
    .keep = "unused"
  )

## Create IDs for task and stimulus
sdt <- sdt |>
  mutate(
    task = str_extract(name, "sick|criminal") |>
      factor(levels = c("sick", "criminal")),
    stim = factor(name),
    .keep = "unused",
    .after = 1
  )

dat_acc <- sdt |>
  summarise(accuracy = sum(accuracy) / n(), .by = c(pid, task))

t.test(filter(dat_acc, task == "sick")$accuracy)

## Calculate SDT metrics (1: Trial outcome)
sdt <- sdt |>
  mutate(
    type = "hit",
    type = ifelse(truth == "Yes" & response == "No", "miss", type),
    type = ifelse(truth == "No" & response == "No", "cr", type),
    type = ifelse(truth == "No" & response == "Yes", "fa", type)
  )
count(sdt, truth, response, type) |>
  mutate(p = percent(n / sum(n)))

## Calculate SDT metrics (2: z scores and parameters)
## Note: we omit the negative sign: negative values of *c* indicate a bias toward responding "No"
sdt <- sdt |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    .by = c(pid, task, type)
  ) |>
  # Make zero counts explicit
  complete(pid, task, type, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(
    hr = hit / (hit + miss),
    fr = fa / (fa + cr),
    # Adjust indeterminate rates
    across(c(hr, fr), ~ if_else(.x == 1, 1 - 1 / (2 * 7), .x)),
    across(c(hr, fr), ~ if_else(.x == 0, 1 / (2 * 7), .x)),
    zhr = qnorm(hr),
    zfr = qnorm(fr),
    dprime = zhr - zfr,
    crit = -(zhr + zfr) / 2
  )

# Other responses

## Take SDT task data out of main data
dat <- dat |>
  select(-contains("_sick_"), -contains("criminal"))

## Scale scores
## Names of all groups
groups <- c(
  "obese",
  "elder",
  "limbs",
  "mark",
  "tb",
  "prison",
  "gay",
  "lesb",
  "home",
  "addict",
  "immig",
  "polit",
  "lawyer"
)

## Rescale all scale items
scl <- dat |>
  select(pid, obese1:pds7) |>
  mutate(
    # Rescale all variables from 1-7 to 0-1
    across(-pid, ~ (.x - 1) / 6),
    # Reverse code positive items group prejudice (1, 2, 4, 5)
    across(
      unlist(map(groups, ~ paste0(.x, c(1, 2, 4, 5)))),
      ~ 1 - .x
    )
  )

## Calculate means over items
scl <- scl |>
  pivot_longer(-pid) |>
  separate(name, c("scale", "item"), sep = -1) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(pid, scale)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = scale, values_from = value)

## Take out scales from main data
dat <- dat |>
  select(-c(obese1:pds7))

# Join to create a table with one row per person
dat <- dat |>
  left_join(scl, by = "pid") |>
  left_join(
    sdt |>
      select(pid, task, dprime, crit) |>
      pivot_wider(names_from = task, values_from = c(dprime, crit)),
    by = "pid"
  ) |>
  select(pid, everything())

# Recode remaining variables
# We were going to code female: -0.5, male 0.5 to center on grand mean,
# but data has four gender categories
# We collapse smallest binary gender
dat <- dat |>
  mutate(
    gender = factor(
      gender,
      levels = 1:4,
      labels = c("Man", "Woman", "Other", "Prefer not to say")
    )
  )
# Lump less frequent levels to min_n(male, female)
dat <- dat |>
  mutate(
    gender = fct_lump_n(
      gender,
      n = 1,
      other_level = levels(fct_infreq(dat$gender))[2]
    )
  )

## Group membership
dat_membership <- select(dat, starts_with("member"))
dat <- select(dat, -starts_with("member"))
names(dat_membership) <- paste0("m_", groups)
# Recode responses Yes: 1, No (and everything else) (0)
dat_membership <- dat_membership |>
  mutate(
    across(everything(), ~ ifelse(.x == 1, 1, NaN) |> replace_na(0))
  )
dat <- bind_cols(dat, dat_membership)

# Gender breakdown
genders <- dat |>
  count(gender) |>
  mutate(gender = fct_na_value_to_level(gender, "Missing")) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  mutate(gender = str_glue("{gender}: {n}")) |>
  pull(gender) |>
  str_to_sentence()

## Remove temporary tables
rm(dat_membership, dat_acc, scl, sdt, sdt_code)

# Save cleaned data
write_csv(dat, "data/data.csv")
```

## Descriptive results

After excluding `{r} s$total_before_exclusions - s$total_after_exclusions` individuals who did not satisfy the inclusion criteria, the final sample consisted of `{r} s$total_after_exclusions` individuals with the following self-reported gender breakdown: `{r} paste0(genders, collapse = ", ")` (we collapsed "Other" and "Prefer not to say" to the latter because our Stage 1 RR treated sex as a binary variable). We summarize the study's key variables in @tbl-desc, and their correlations in @tbl-cor. We conducted all analyses in R and used the marginaleffects package for testing slopes and their contrasts, and tidyverse for data cleaning and visualization [@r2024; @me2024; @tidyverse2019].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-desc
#| tbl-cap: Descriptives of key variables.

dat |>
  select(
    crit_sick,
    crit_criminal,
    all_of(groups[1:4]),
    pds,
    age
  ) |>
  datasummary_skim(
    output = "tinytable",
    fun_numeric = list(
      M = mean,
      SD = sd,
      Min = min,
      max = Max,
      Histogram = \(x) "",
      `% Missing` = PercentMissing
    )
  ) |>
  style_tt(
    align = "l",
    fontsize = 0.75
  )
```

Notably, @tbl-cor shows that the decision criteria for the two detection tasks were moderately positively correlated, and that prejudice toward all four key target groups were moderately positively intercorrelated. Pairwise correlations between decision criteria in the sickness detection task and prejudice toward the four key groups were not statistically significant. Age correlated negatively with prejudice toward elderly people and individuals with physical disability.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cor
#| tbl-cap: Correlation matrix of key variables.

dat |>
  select(
    c_sick = crit_sick,
    c_crim = crit_criminal,
    all_of(groups[1:4]),
    pds,
    age
  ) |>
  correlation(p_adjust = "none") |>
  datasummary_correlation(output = "tinytable", stars = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(
    align = "l",
    fontsize = 0.75
  )
```

## Hypothesis tests

### H1: Prejudice toward groups with superficially anomalous appearance

We then turned to our main hypothesis (H1) test, that a liberal infectious disease decision criterion---a tendency to respond "Sick"---would correlate with prejudice toward people with obesity, elderly people, people with a physical disability, and people with a facial disfigurement. We regressed, in separate models, prejudice scores for these groups on decision criteria *c* from the sickness detection task. Due to reported gender differences in disgust sensitivity, we included gender (coded as woman: -0.5, man: 0.5) as a covariate to reduce residual variance. We report the key regression parameters in the first four rows of @fig-coef (left; red), @tbl-t1, and visualize all bivariate relations in @fig-scatter.

Note that we calculated the criterion as $c = -\frac{\Phi^{-1}(HR) + \Phi^{-1}(FAR)}{2}$, and thus negative values of *c* indicate a ("liberal") bias toward responding "Yes" [sick / not criminal], and positive values indicate a ("conservative") bias toward responding "No" [healthy / not criminal]. While our Stage 1 RR discussed the hypotheses in this manner, we had inadvertently omitted the negative sign in the formula for *c*. H1 would thus be supported by negative regression coefficients of *c*~infected~ in predicting prejudice toward the four target groups.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: Scatterplots and regression lines (with 95%CIs) for each prejudice scale on signal detection criteria in the contagion detection task. Points are jittered to reduce overplotting.
#| fig-height: 4.8

dat |>
  select(pid, gender, crit_sick, all_of(groups)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(groups)) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = groups)) |>
  ggplot(aes(crit_sick, value)) +
  coord_cartesian(
    ylim = 0:1
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(
    palette = "Set1",
    aesthetics = c("color", "fill")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    "Criterion [infected]"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    "Prejudice",
    breaks = c(0, .2, .4, .6, .8, 1),
  ) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = .2,
    size = .15,
    position = position_jitter(.075, .025)
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    col = "black"
  ) +
  facet_wrap("name", ncol = 5)
```

```{r}
#| label: models-fit

# Code variables for models
contrasts(dat$gender) <- c(-0.5, 0.5)
dat$age <- dat$age - mean(dat$age)

# Fit all regressions
dat_fit <- tibble(
  group = groups,
  # Analysis 1
  fit1 = map(
    group,
    ~ lm(str_glue("{.x} ~ crit_sick + gender"), data = dat)
  ),
  fit1sex = map(
    group,
    ~ lm(str_glue("{.x} ~ crit_sick * gender"), data = dat)
  ),
  # Analysis 2
  # Models without people not members in that category
  fit2 = map(
    group,
    ~ lm(
      str_glue("{.x} ~ crit_sick + gender"),
      data = filter(dat, get(paste0("m_", .x)) != 1)
    )
  ),
  fit2sex = map(
    group,
    ~ lm(
      str_glue("{.x} ~ crit_sick * gender"),
      data = filter(dat, get(paste0("m_", .x)) != 1)
    )
  ),
  # Analysis 3 and 4
  # Adjusting for Ccriminal
  fit3 = map(
    group,
    ~ lm(str_glue("{.x} ~ crit_sick + gender + crit_criminal"), data = dat)
  ),
  fit3sex = map(
    group,
    ~ lm(str_glue("{.x} ~ crit_sick * gender + crit_criminal"), data = dat)
  ),
)

# Determine if (sex * crit_sick) is significant
# and pick appropriate model for each test
dat_fit <- dat_fit |>
  mutate(
    across(
      ends_with("sex"),
      ~ map_lgl(
        .x,
        ~ summary(.x)$coefficients[
          "crit_sick:gender1",
          "Pr(>|t|)"
        ] <=
          0.05
      ),
      .names = "i{str_extract(.col, '[0-9]')}"
    ),
    # Pick interaction model if its significant
    m1 = if_else(i1, fit1sex, fit1),
    m2 = if_else(i2, fit2sex, fit2),
    m3 = if_else(i3, fit3sex, fit3),
  ) |>
  # Discard unnecessary models & variables
  select(group, i1, i2, i3, m1, m2, m3)

# Conduct all tests
# T1: Baseline OR separate gender coef if interaction is significant
# T2: T1 but exclude participants who identify with target group
# T3: T1 but adjust for crit_criminal
# T4: T3 where we test crit_sick > gender AND crit_sick > crit_criminal

dat_fit <- dat_fit |>
  mutate(
    t1 = map(m1, ~ .avg_slopes(.x)),
    t2 = map(m2, ~ .avg_slopes(.x)),
    t3 = map(m3, ~ .avg_slopes(.x)),
    t4 = map(
      m3,
      ~ avg_slopes(
        .x,
        df = .x$df.residual,
        hypothesis = c(
          `c_sick - gender` = "crit_sick - gender = 0",
          `c_sick - c_crim` = "crit_sick - crit_criminal = 0"
        )
      )
    )
  )

# If interaction is non-significant, gender slopes are identical
# so here we pick first to represent both
dat_fit <- dat_fit |>
  mutate(
    t1 = if_else(i1, t1, map(t1, ~ slice(.x, 1))),
    t2 = if_else(i2, t2, map(t2, ~ slice(.x, 1))),
    t3 = if_else(i3, t3, map(t3, ~ slice(.x, 1)))
    # t4 is done without interaction
  )
```

Of the four key target groups, *c*~infected~ had a statistically significant negative relation only with prejudice toward individuals with a facial disfigurement (@fig-coef, row 4, red ["Test 1"]; @tbl-t1). Note that the interaction between gender and *c*~infected~ was not significant in predicting prejudice toward any of the four key groups, and therefore in @fig-coef and @tbl-t1 we only report a common coefficient for these groups.

```{r}
#| label: fig-coef
#| fig-cap: "Key regression slopes (left; tests 1-3) and contrasts (right; contrasting slope of Csick with Ccrim and gender) for all 13 target groups. Filled points indicate statistically significant negative coefficients (Slopes: one-sided p-value; Contrasts: two-sided p-value), empty points indicate non-significant coefficients. Circles: Both genders or Women; Squares: Men."
#| fig-height: 3.4

dat_fit |>
  mutate(group = fct_inorder(group) |> fct_rev()) |>
  select(group, t1:t4) |>
  pivot_longer(-group) |>
  unnest(value) |>
  mutate(
    term = if_else(!is.na(term), "Slope", "Contrast"),
    name = if_else(!is.na(hypothesis), hypothesis, name) |>
      factor(
        levels = c("t1", "t2", "t3", "c_sick - c_crim", "c_sick - gender"),
        labels = c("1", "2", "3", "Csick - Ccrim", "Csick - gender")
      ) |>
      fct_rev(),
    p.value = coalesce(p.value.nonsup, p.value),
    gender = if_else(!is.na(gender), gender, "Woman"),
    sig = p.value <= 0.05,
    p.group = interaction(name, gender),
    shape = interaction(sig, gender)
  ) |>
  select(group, term, name, gender, estimate:conf.high, sig, p.group, shape) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = estimate,
      y = group,
      color = name,
      group = p.group
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    "Estimate [95% CI]"
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(
      "FALSE.Woman" = "circle filled",
      "TRUE.Woman" = "circle",
      "FALSE.Man" = "square filled",
      "TRUE.Man" = "square"
    )
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(
    "Test",
    palette = "Set1",
    direction = -1
  ) +
  guides(shape = "none", color = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2, linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(
      xmin = conf.low,
      xmax = conf.high,
      shape = shape
    ),
    fill = "white",
    linewidth = .5,
    fatten = 3,
    position = position_dodge2(width = .8, preserve = "single")
  ) +
  facet_manual("term", design = c("BBBAA"), scales = "free") +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
```

Following our protocol, we then examined the regression coefficients in models that excluded participants who self-identified with the target group ("Test 2"); adjusted for *c*~criminal~ ("Test 3"); and compared *c*~infected~ with *c*~criminal~ and the gender coefficient ("Test 4"). The key regression coefficients from models that excluded participants self-identifying with the target group are shown in blue in @fig-coef ("Test 2"; see also @tbl-t2): Results did not differ from those of the main analysis.

When adjusting for *c*~criminal~ ("Test 3"), the results were qualitatively similar, with the key difference that the relationship between *c*~infected~ and prejudice toward individuals with a facial disfigurement was no longer statistically significant (@fig-coef green; see also @tbl-t3). Finally, we tested the regression coefficient for *c*~infected~ against that of gender and *c*~criminal~ (analysis 4; @fig-coef "Contrast"; see also @tbl-t4). The slope of *c*~infected~ was consistently smaller than the prejudice gender difference (recall we coded Woman: -0.5 and Man: 0.5), and smaller than the slope of *c*~criminal~ for prejudice toward obese individuals, but not significantly different for the three other groups.

Overall, then, across the four target groups and four analyses, we found at best weak evidence for the smoke-detector principle.

### H2: Prejudice toward groups included in detection task

Next, we turned to H2, whether the smoke detector principle holds for the social group for which the response bias was measured (@fig-coef left, "tb" and "prison"; @tbl-t1 - @tbl-t4). *c*~infected~ predicted prejudice toward criminals (in analyses 1 & 2) but not toward individuals with infectious disease. The coefficient for *c*~infected~ was not statistically significantly different from those of *c*~criminal~ or gender (@fig-coef right). Thus, we did not find support for the hypothesis.

### H3: Prejudice toward groups where prejudice is putatively motivated by pathogen avoidance, but not based on anomalous appearance

We found that a liberal decision criterion in the infectious disease detection task was correlated with prejudice toward gay men and lesbian women. These results were similar across Tests 1 - 3 (@fig-coef "Slope"). However, the coefficients were less negative than those associated with either gender or *c*~criminal~ (@fig-coef "Contrast").

*c*~infected~ was not a statistically significant predictor of prejudice toward either homeless individuals or drug addicts, but negatively associated with prejudice toward immigrants among women and not statistically significant among men.

### H4: Prejudice toward common targets

Those with a more liberal bias toward responding "sick" in the infectious disease detection task reported lower levels of prejudice toward politicians and lawyers (the latter was positive and statistically significant only in Test 3).

## Exploratory analyses

### Disgust sensitivity

We then estimated pairwise Pearson correlations between signal detection parameters from the infectious disease detection task, prejudice, and pathogen disgust sensitivity. We report these results in @fig-pds.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pds
#| fig-cap: "Correlations between pathogen disgust sensitivity and SDT parameters & prejudice scores."
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-width: 3.8

dat |>
  select(pid, crit_sick, dprime_sick, any_of(groups), pds) |>
  correlation(p_adjust = "none") |>
  filter(Parameter2 == "pds") |>
  mutate(
    Parameter1 = factor(
      Parameter1,
      c(groups, "crit_sick", "dprime_sick")
    ) |>
      fct_rev(),
    sig = p <= 0.05
  ) |>
  tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(r, Parameter1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    "Pearson r [95%CI]"
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "circle filled", "TRUE" = "circle")
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = 2,
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(xmin = CI_low, xmax = CI_high, shape = sig),
    fill = "white",
    linewidth = .5,
    fatten = 3
  ) +
  guides(shape = "none") +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_blank()
  )
```

### Hypothesis test

We then considered an alternative analytic approach for testing the overall hypothesis that a liberal infectious disease decision criterion is associated with prejudice toward particular social groups. Above, we tested this idea separately for multiple target groups. Here, we model the relationship between *c*~infected~ and prejudice across target groups in one multilevel model to accomplish three goals: (A) Estimate an average relation between *c*~infected~ and prejudice across target groups; (B) avoid overfitting target-group-specific relations using partial pooling; and (C) evaluate evidence for the null hypothesis that the average relationship between *c*~infected~ and prejudice is zero using a bayes factor approximated with the Savage-Dickey density ratio [@wagenmakersBayesianHypothesisTesting2010].

We modeled the z-scored prejudice rating P for the *i*th participant and *j*th target group with a standard multilevel model specified as

$$
\begin{align}
\text{P}_{ij} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(\eta_{ij}, \sigma^2), \\
\eta_{ij} &= \beta_0 + \gamma_{0j} + \delta_{0i} + \beta_1\text{G}_{ij} +
  (\beta_2 + \gamma_{1j})\text{C}_{ij}, \\
\begin{bmatrix}
  \gamma_0 \\ \gamma_1
\end{bmatrix} & \sim
\operatorname{MVN}\left(
  \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix},
  \begin{pmatrix}
    \tau_0 & \\
    \rho &\tau_1
  \end{pmatrix}
\right), \\
\delta_0 &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \tau_{\delta}), \\
\beta_1 &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \phi).
\end{align}
$$

Above, we denote prejudice as P, gender (woman: -0.5, man: 0.5) as G, and *c*~infected~ as C. $\beta_2$ and $\gamma_1$ are the population-level, and target-group-specific, regression slopes of prejudice on *c*~infected~, respectively. Critically, because we could not determine an exact prediction for the average effect size based on previous work or theory, we estimated the model across a range of priors $\phi \in \{0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1\}$. For the other model parameters, we used the brms' package's default priors [@brms2017; @brms2018].

```{r}
#| label: fit-glmm
library(brms)
library(cmdstanr)
# Model estimation options, customize in .Renviron
dir.create("cache", FALSE)
options(
  brms.backend = Sys.getenv("BRMS_BACKEND", "rstan"),
  brms.threads = as.numeric(Sys.getenv("BRMS_THREADS"), 1),
  mc.cores = as.numeric(Sys.getenv("MAX_CORES"), 4)
)

# Reshape data for multilevel model and z-score prejudice scores
# Don't include tb and prison targets
dat_b <- dat |>
  select(pid, gender, age, crit_sick, all_of(groups), -tb, -prison) |>
  mutate(across(any_of(groups), ~ scale(.) |> as.numeric())) |>
  pivot_longer(any_of(groups), names_to = "target", values_to = "prejudice")

# Specify model
bform <- bf(
  prejudice ~ gender + crit_sick + (1 | pid) + (1 + crit_sick | target)
)

fits <- tibble(
  phi = number(c(.1, .25, .5, .75, 1)),
  prior = str_glue("normal(0,{phi})"),
  fit = map2(
    prior,
    phi,
    ~ brm(
      bform,
      data = dat_b,
      prior = prior_string(.x, class = "b", coef = "crit_sick"),
      iter = 4000,
      warmup = 1000,
      file = str_glue("cache/brm-phi-{.y}"),
      control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
      file_refit = "never",
      sample_prior = "yes"
    )
  )
)

fits <- fits |>
  mutate(
    fixef = map(
      fit,
      ~ hypothesis(.x, "crit_sick = 0")
    ),
    coef = map(
      fit,
      ~ hypothesis(
        .x,
        "crit_sick = 0",
        scope = "coef",
        group = "target"
      )$hypothesis
    ),
    .keep = "unused"
  )

x <- rope(fits$fixef[[5]]$samples$H1, range = c(-0.1, 0.1))
x <- percent(x$ROPE_Percentage, .1)
```

We show the results of this analysis in @fig-bf. First, the estimated relation between *c*~infected~ and prejudice toward the "average" target group from the multilevel model ("Pooled") is shown as a light gray density. We show the parameters in @fig-bf (left) for $\phi=1$ because the estimates did not meaningfully differ across these prior specifications. The average relation is neglibly small and closely centered on zero (with `{r} x` of the posterior distribution within [-0.1, 0.1]), suggesting that practically meaningfully large relations are very unlikely.

Second, the filled points and intervals show the partially pooled estimates of $\gamma_1$ in visual comparison to their fixed effects counterparts from our main analysis (empty circles; @fig-bf). We connected these with vertical lines to illustrate how partial pooling has slightly shrunk the most extreme estimates toward the mean, and subsequently provided more accurate estimates that avoid overfitting.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bf
#| fig-cap: "Results from multilevel model assessing the relationship between Csick and prejudice across target groups. Left: Posterior density of the Csick - prejudice [average] relationship in gray. We shaded this density as darker for |x| > 0.1. Filled points indicate partially pooled target-group-specific estimates from multilevel model. Empty points indicate fixed-effect target-group-specific estimates of the corresponding models discussed in the main text. Note for the models here, we standardized prejudice scores. Right: Evidence ratio favoring the point null over the alternative (relationship is non-null), as a function of the standard deviation of the prior distribution on the average relationship."
#| fig-height: 2.2

# Refit stdz FE models
fits_lm <- tibble(
  Group = groups[!(groups %in% c("tb", "prison"))],
  lm = map(
    Group,
    ~ tidy(
      lm(
        str_glue("scale({.x}) ~ crit_sick + gender"),
        data = dat
      ),
      conf.int = TRUE
    ) |>
      filter(term == "crit_sick") |>
      select(lm.e = estimate, lm.cl = conf.low, lm.ul = conf.high)
  )
) |>
  unnest(lm)

# Wrangle, order, give y-coords
fits_lm <- fits_lm |>
  arrange(lm.e) |>
  mutate(
    lm.g = fct_inorder(Group),
    lm.y = (as.numeric(lm.g) - 5.5) / 200
  )
fits_coef <- fits |>
  filter(phi == "1.00") |>
  select(coef) |>
  unnest(coef) |>
  arrange(Estimate) |>
  mutate(
    coef.g = fct_inorder(Group),
    coef.y = .25 + (as.numeric(coef.g) - 5.5) / 200
  ) |>
  left_join(fits_lm)
fits_fixef <- fits |>
  filter(phi == "1.00") |>
  select(fixef) |>
  mutate(fixef = map(fixef, ~ .x$samples)) |>
  unnest(fixef)

pa <- fits_coef |>
  ggplot() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, .3),
    labels = c("Fixed", "Pooled"),
    expand = expansion(c(.001, .025))
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    "Estimate",
    expand = expansion(.1)
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("gray25", "gray75"),
    aesthetics = c("slab_fill")
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    lty = 2,
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  stat_slab(
    data = fits_fixef,
    height = .15,
    slab_alpha = 0.75,
    slab_linewidth = 0.25,
    slab_color = "black",
    .width = c(.8, .95),
    aes(x = H1, y = .3, slab_fill = after_stat(between(x, -0.1, 0.1)))
  ) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(
      x = Estimate,
      xmin = CI.Lower,
      xmax = CI.Upper,
      y = coef.y,
      group = coef.g
    ),
    position = position_dodge(.1),
    fatten = 2,
    linewidth = .2
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = Estimate, xend = lm.e, y = coef.y, yend = lm.y),
    linewidth = .25
  ) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(lm.e, xmin = lm.cl, xmax = lm.ul, y = lm.y, group = lm.g),
    position = position_dodge(.1),
    fill = "white",
    shape = 21,
    fatten = 2.25,
    linewidth = .2,
    stroke = .75
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  )

pb <- fits |>
  mutate(fixef = map(fixef, ~ .x$hypothesis)) |>
  select(phi, fixef) |>
  unnest(fixef) |>
  ggplot(aes(phi, Evid.Ratio)) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    "Prior SD (phi)"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    "Evid. Ratio H0/HA",
    limits = c(0, 20)
  ) +
  geom_line(
    linewidth = .33,
    group = 1
  ) +
  geom_point()

(pa | pb) + plot_layout(widths = c(7, 3))
```

Third, the right panel of @fig-bf shows the evidence ratio between H0: $\beta_2 = 0$ and HA: $\beta_2 \neq 0$. Across the prior distributions that we considered, the evidence for the null hypothesis ranged from weak to very strong. We note that our numerical approximations to the evidence ratio are necessarily tentative because the prior distribution for $\beta_2$ is underdetermined by current theory but nevertheless take them to indicate evidence against the smoke detector principle.
